title: Krupski v. Costa Crociere S.p.A. (2010)
summary: Knowing that two companies existed did not foreclose a mistake about which company should have been sued.
notes:
Relation back has additional requirements, including notice, lack of prejudice in defending, and the relation of the amended claim to the original transaction. This case resolves the mistake inquiry; it does not eliminate the other requirements.

Justice Sotomayor wrote for the Court; Justice Scalia concurred in part, declining to rely on the Advisory Committee Notes. Krupski's ticket named Costa Cruise (the U.S. sales agent) on the front but identified Costa Crociere as carrier on the back; she sued Costa Cruise three weeks before the one-year limitations period ran.

sections.Parties: Krupski, an injured cruise passenger, initially sued Costa Cruise Lines and later sought to substitute Costa Crociere, the carrier.
sections.Material Facts: The ticket and related information identified two associated entities with different roles. Krupski sued the United States sales and marketing entity rather than the Italian carrier responsible for operating the cruise. The original defendant pointed out the distinction. After the limitations period, she amended to name the carrier. The issue was whether the carrier understood within the required notice period that the action would have targeted it but for the confusion about identity or roles.
sections.Procedural History: The district court denied relation back and entered judgment for the carrier. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, emphasizing the plaintiff’s knowledge and delay. The Supreme Court reversed and remanded.
sections.Issue: Did the plaintiff’s awareness of the carrier’s existence prevent relation back under Rule 15(c)(1)(C)?
sections.Holding: No. The inquiry concerned what the correct defendant knew or should have known about the mistake, not simply whether the plaintiff knew its name existed.
sections.Reasoning: A plaintiff can know of an entity yet misunderstand its role in the events. The rule protects defendants from untimely surprise through timely notice and knowledge that a mistake explains their omission. It therefore directs attention to the prospective defendant’s understanding, rather than making the plaintiff’s diligence a separate decisive condition. A deliberate choice between correctly understood defendants differs from a mistake about which entity was responsible. The lower courts’ focus on the plaintiff’s knowledge of the name did not apply that distinction properly.

learning.why: Knowing that two companies existed did not foreclose a mistake about which company should have been sued.

topics.cp-relation-back: The correct defendant’s timely understanding of the mistake controlled the relation-back inquiry.
topics.cp-notice: The rule protects a newly named defendant through notice and knowledge within the specified period.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: Relation back determines timeliness of the amended claim, rather than whether the cruise operator was negligent.
topics.cp-frcp-15: The holding construes Rule 15(c)(1)(C)'s mistake-of-identity requirement.
topics.cp-limitations: Relation back matters only because the one-year limitations period had run before the correct carrier was named.
